patient.chief_complaint: Progressive memory loss and word-finding difficulty over 18 months, with new episodic confusion
patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Gerald Hoffman is a 72-year-old right-handed retired principal who presents to the neurology memory clinic accompanied by his wife, Eleanor, for evaluation of progressive memory difficulties over the past 18 months. His wife first noticed the changes approximately 18 months ago when he began forgetting recent conversations and misplacing items with increasing frequency — he would put keys in the refrigerator and forget where he had stored gardening tools he had used the day before. His longtime interest in crossword puzzles, which he previously completed in ink, has become notably more labored, and he now leaves many incomplete. Over the subsequent year his word-finding difficulties worsened: he frequently struggles to retrieve proper names and low-frequency nouns, sometimes describing rather than naming objects. His wife notes he has become repetitive, asking the same question within an hour.

In the past 2-3 months, new symptoms emerged that concern his wife: she has observed several episodes of blank staring lasting 5-10 seconds during which he does not respond, then resumes activity without any memory of the pause. These occur several times per week. He has also twice reported seeing something that was not there — once a small animal in the kitchen, and once a shadow in the examination room today. He has been somewhat more withdrawn and less interested in social activities, which Eleanor attributes to frustration with his memory. He denies feeling depressed. Sleep is adequate with good CPAP adherence; wife has not observed acting-out of dreams or nocturnal vocalizations. He remains independent in basic ADLs including bathing, dressing, and grooming. He stopped driving one month ago at Eleanor's request after he missed a turn on a familiar route and drove in the wrong direction for several minutes.

The family history is notable for an older brother with diagnosed Parkinson's disease, which Eleanor has read about and wonders whether her husband might have something similar. On careful questioning, she confirms that his personality is unchanged, there has been no new urinary urgency or incontinence, and no falls. He has not had obvious tremor at rest.

results.title: Sensitivity and specificity of 123I-FP-CIT SPECT in dementia with Lewy bodies and Alzheimer disease
results.authors: McKeith I, O'Brien J, Walker Z, et al. (NICE-DLB study group)
results.summary: Multicenter study (n=326) demonstrated that 123I-FP-CIT SPECT (DaTscan) has 77.7% sensitivity and 90.4% specificity for distinguishing DLB from AD and other dementias. A normal DaTscan makes DLB substantially less likely and, combined with clinical and biomarker data, supports an alternative diagnosis. DaTscan is listed as a supportive biomarker for DLB in diagnostic criteria.

results.title: Diagnosis and management of dementia with Lewy bodies: Fourth consensus report of the DLB Consortium
results.authors: McKeith IG, Boeve BF, Dickson DW, et al.
results.summary: Fourth consensus criteria for DLB. Core clinical features: fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, and one or more parkinsonism features. Indicative biomarkers include reduced dopamine transporter uptake on SPECT or PET (DaTscan). A normal DaTscan in a patient with soft core features substantially reduces the probability of DLB. Diagnosis requires at least two core features or one core feature with one indicative biomarker.

results.title: Usefulness of DaTscan in differentiating dementia with Lewy bodies from Alzheimer disease
results.authors: Walker Z, Costa DC, Walker RW, et al.
results.journal: Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery and Psychiatry
results.summary: Prospective study found that a normal DaTscan in clinically uncertain dementia cases (with some Lewy body features) reliably excluded DLB at post-mortem validation and correctly pointed toward AD or other non-DLB dementias. A positive amyloid biomarker with normal DaTscan provides convergent evidence for AD rather than DLB.

output.summary: DaTscan (123I-ioflupane SPECT) measures presynaptic dopamine transporter availability and is a DLB indicative biomarker. In patients with dementia and overlapping AD/DLB features, a normal DaTscan substantially reduces the probability of DLB (specificity ~90%). However, DaTscan does not diagnose AD; it is used to exclude DLB. Definitive AD diagnosis requires positive amyloid biomarkers (CSF or amyloid PET) combined with compatible clinical presentation. Concurrent positive amyloid PET or CSF ATN profile with a normal DaTscan provides convergent support for AD rather than DLB in patients presenting with mixed features.

critical_actions: Order DaTscan to evaluate for presynaptic dopaminergic deficit when DLB is actively on the differential due to soft features (cognitive fluctuation, possible visual misperception, mild rigidity); a normal DaTscan argues strongly against DLB
Confirm AD diagnosis with positive amyloid biomarkers (CSF ATN profile or amyloid PET) rather than relying solely on soft DLB-suggestive features to drive diagnosis
Obtain collateral history from an informant to characterize the fluctuation pattern, hallucinations, and RBD features — all core DLB criteria that must be formally assessed
Exclude reversible causes of cognitive decline with screening labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate)
Obtain structural brain MRI with dementia protocol to assess medial temporal atrophy and evaluate basal ganglia/substantia nigra
Quantify cognitive impairment with formal neuropsychological testing to characterize the domain profile
Assess safety: driving, medication management, finances, and need for caregiver support
contraindicated_actions: Do not diagnose DLB based on soft clinical features alone (isolated mild fluctuation, a single unconfirmed visual misperception, mild bilateral cogwheel rigidity) when DaTscan is normal — a normal DaTscan argues strongly against DLB
Do not initiate antipsychotics in this patient until DLB has been formally excluded, given the risk of severe antipsychotic sensitivity reactions in DLB
Do not prescribe anticholinergic medications which worsen cognition in patients with AD
Do not start memantine monotherapy at the mild dementia stage; memantine is approved for moderate-to-severe AD

Do not attribute the cognitive fluctuations exclusively to DLB without DaTscan evidence — brief blank-staring episodes can occur in AD-related attentional fluctuation and require clinical contextualization
key_reasoning_points: This case has soft DLB-suggestive features (cognitive fluctuations, one possible visual misperception, mild bilateral cogwheel rigidity with family history of PD) that appropriately raise DLB on the differential — making DaTscan clinically justified

A normal DaTscan (no presynaptic dopaminergic deficit) argues strongly against DLB; per 2017 DLB Consortium criteria, DaTscan is an indicative biomarker and a normal result substantially reduces DLB probability
DaTscan cannot diagnose AD — it excludes DLB; convergent positive amyloid biomarkers (CSF A+T+ and positive amyloid PET) are required to confirm AD pathology

The amnestic-predominant cognitive profile (severe storage-type memory failure with minimal cue benefit, bilateral MTA grade 2, multi-domain involvement) is the hallmark of typical AD rather than DLB, which classically leads with visuospatial and attentional deficits

Mild bilateral cogwheel rigidity on examination with a family history of Parkinson's disease is a red herring anchoring toward DLB or PDD, but rigidity alone without established motor PD syndrome and with normal DaTscan is insufficient for DLB diagnosis
A single, isolated possible visual misperception does not meet the threshold for 'recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations' required as a DLB core feature

metadata.real_seed_note: A systematic PMC search for a published CC-BY open-access case report of confirmed AD with DLB differential and normal DaTscan did not yield a verified, unambiguously CC-BY case meeting all criteria (72-year-old male, amnestic AD, normal DaTscan excluding DLB). This case was therefore authored as an authentic, clinically representative AD-vs-DLB puzzle consistent with published diagnostic criteria (NIA-AA 2011/2018, DLB Consortium 2017 McKeith et al. Neurology) without a specific PMID seed. The scenario is grounded in real-world clinical patterns documented in the DaTscan AD/DLB literature.
metadata.clinical_notes: Diagnostic puzzle case: amnestic AD in which soft DLB features (mild fluctuation, one possible visual misperception, mild bilateral cogwheel rigidity, family history of PD in a sibling) appropriately raise DLB on the differential. The correct diagnostic trajectory requires ordering DaTscan (clinically justified — not useless here), interpreting a normal result as arguing against DLB, then confirming AD with positive CSF/amyloid PET biomarkers. This is the first case in the v5 ALZ-EARLY set with a DaTscan as a load-bearing recommended tool.
teaching_points: DaTscan is indicated (not useless) when DLB is a genuine clinical consideration — soft features suffice to justify the test
A normal DaTscan is a strong argument against DLB but does not itself diagnose AD
Positive amyloid biomarkers (CSF ATN or amyloid PET) are required to confirm AD pathology
Single unverified visual misperceptions and attentional fluctuation in an elderly person do not fulfill DLB core diagnostic criteria
Mild bilateral cogwheel rigidity without established PD motor syndrome and with normal DaTscan is insufficient for DLB diagnosis
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Diagnostic puzzle: soft DLB-suggestive features (fluctuation, visual misperception, mild rigidity, PD family history) anchor toward DLB; correct resolution requires DaTscan (justified), interpreting normal DaTscan as arguing against DLB, and confirming AD via positive CSF ATN + amyloid PET; single-slot mock-server limitation noted for dual advanced imaging
